LEGAL NOTE — Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 (Machinery Regulation): date of application and status of Directive 2006/42/EC as at 17 November 2026

BOTTOM LINE
1. Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 applies from 20 January 2027 (general date of application, Art. 54, second paragraph, as corrected).
2. Directive 2006/42/EC ceases to apply on 20 January 2027 (Art. 51(2), as corrected: 'repealed with effect from 20 January 2027'). It therefore applies until and including 19 January 2027.
3. As at today, 17 November 2026, Directive 2006/42/EC is STILL IN FORCE. The repeal is future-dated; it has not yet taken effect.

1. THE GOVERNING TEXT
1.1 The act. Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 June 2023 on machinery and repealing Directive 2006/42/EC and Council Directive 73/361/EEC, OJ L 165, 29.6.2023, p. 1. It is directly applicable in all Member States and required no transposition.
1.2 The correction. Corrigendum of 4 July 2023, OJ L 169, 4.7.2023, pp. 35-36, published in all 24 language versions. It is this corrected text, not the text as printed in OJ L 165, that is the authentic text. The relevant items:
   - Item 5: 'On page 38, Article 51, paragraph 2, first subparagraph: for: "14 January 2027", read: "20 January 2027".'
   - Item 6: 'On page 38, Article 52, paragraph 1, first sentence: for: "14 January 2027", read: "20 January 2027".'
   - Item 7: 'On page 38, Article 52, paragraph 1, second sentence: for: "13 July 2023", read: "19 July 2023".'
   The same 14th-to-20th shift is carried through the remaining Article 54 dates (items 1-4 and the corresponding item for Art. 54). The fetched corrigendum extract is truncated after item 7, so the Article 54 item is not quoted verbatim here; the corrected Article 54 date is instead taken from the consolidated version and the EUR-Lex 'Dates' table (point 3 below). Nothing in the answer depends on that item, because Art. 51(2) and Art. 52(1) are corrected on the face of items 5 and 6.
1.3 Consequence of a corrigendum. A corrigendum corrects the published text with retroactive effect to the date of publication of the original act; the erroneous version is not a valid competing text. Any reading of the Regulation that uses '14 January 2027' is reading the superseded, uncorrected OJ L 165 text and is wrong for any date after 4 July 2023.

2. THE OPERATIVE PROVISIONS (CORRECTED TEXT)
Art. 54, first paragraph: entry into force on the twentieth day following publication (published 29 June 2023, so entry into force 19 July 2023).
Art. 54, second paragraph: 'It shall apply from 20 January 2027.'
Art. 54, third paragraph, partial application dates (corrected):
   (a) Articles 26-42 from 20 January 2024;
   (b) Article 50(1) from 20 October 2023;
   (c) Article 6(7) and Articles 48 and 52 from 19 July 2023;
   (d) Article 6(2)-(6), (8) and (11) and Articles 47 and 53(3) from 20 July 2024.
Art. 51(2), first subparagraph: 'Directive 2006/42/EC is repealed with effect from 20 January 2027.' Second subparagraph: references to the repealed Directive are to be read as references to the Regulation, per the correlation table in Annex XII.
Art. 51(1): Council Directive 73/361/EEC is repealed (no deferred date; repealed on the Regulation's entry into force, 19 July 2023).

3. CORROBORATION OF 20 JANUARY 2027 (three independent sources)
(a) EUR-Lex act page, 'Dates' block for CELEX 32023R1230 (current consolidated version 27/07/2026): 'Date of effect: 20/01/2027; Application; See Art 54'; and the partial dates 19/07/2023, 20/01/2024, 20/07/2024, 20/10/2026. It also records 'Repeal 32006L0042 — 20/01/2027' in the relationships table.
(b) Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2026/2015 of 4 September 2026, OJ L, 7.9.2026 (ELI dec_impl/2026/2015): recital 14 — 'Given that Directive 2006/42/EC is repealed by Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 ... with effect from 20 January 2027, it is necessary to repeal, with effect from that date, Implementing Decision (EU) 2023/1586'; Art. 2 — 'Implementing Decision (EU) 2023/1586 is repealed with effect from 20 January 2027.' A Commission act adopted in September 2026 is contemporaneous, authoritative confirmation that the operative date is 20 January 2027.
(c) EUR-Lex summary of Directive 2006/42/EC (CELEX 32006L0042): 'Directive 2006/42/EC is repealed and replaced by Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 ... as of 20 January 2027'; and 'The directive has been repealed by Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 ..., although it will remain applicable until 19 January 2027.'
The only source in the corpus that says '14 January 2027' is the uncorrected original text (OJ L 165 PDF/HTML), which the corrigendum displaced.

4. ANSWER TO ASK 3 — IS THE DIRECTIVE STILL IN FORCE TODAY?
Yes. On 17 November 2026 the repeal in Art. 51(2) has not yet taken effect: 17 November 2026 precedes 20 January 2027. The Directive is therefore in force today and remains the applicable legal framework for new machinery until and including 19 January 2027. Two refinements a lawyer should record:
(a) The Directive in force today is the Directive as amended, most recently by Directive (EU) 2024/2749 of 9 October 2024 (OJ L, 2024/2749, 8.11.2024), whose transposition deadline was 29 May 2026 and whose rules apply from 30 May 2026 (internal-market-emergency procedures for conformity assessment, presumption of conformity, common specifications and market surveillance). Those amendments do not touch the repeal date.
(b) The Directive is 'in force' but 'repealed with effect from' a future date — the two are not in tension; Art. 51(2) is a deferred repeal, effective on the Regulation's general application date.

5. WHAT 'APPLIES FROM 20 JANUARY 2027' DOES AND DOES NOT MEAN
5.1 It is the general date of application. Parts of the Regulation already apply: Art. 6(7), Arts. 48 and 52 since 19 July 2023; Art. 50(1) since 20 October 2023; Arts. 26-42 (conformity assessment bodies/notified bodies) since 20 January 2024; Art. 6(2)-(6), (8), (11), Arts. 47 and 53(3) since 20 July 2024. So the precise statement is: full application from 20 January 2027, with the listed provisions applicable earlier.
5.2 It is not the entry-into-force date. The Regulation entered into force on 19 July 2023 (Art. 54, first paragraph). The Directive's repeal is tied to the application date, not the entry-into-force date; conflating the two is the most common error in secondary commentary.
5.3 Transitional provisions (Art. 52, as corrected) do not postpone the repeal date; they preserve market access for legacy goods:
   - Art. 52(1): Member States shall not impede the making available on the market of products placed on the market in conformity with Directive 2006/42/EC before 20 January 2027. However, Chapter VI of the Regulation (Union market surveillance and Union safeguard procedure) applies mutatis mutandis to such products from 19 July 2023 in place of Art. 11 of the Directive, including products for which a procedure under Art. 11 has already begun.
   - Art. 52(2): EC type-examination certificates and approval decisions issued under Art. 12 of the Directive remain valid until they expire.
   Practical effect: a machine lawfully placed on the EU market on or before 19 January 2027 may continue to be made available down the distribution chain after 20 January 2027; a machine first placed on the market on or after 20 January 2027 must comply with the Regulation.

6. POST-2023 AMENDMENTS CHECKED (none moves the date)
- Regulation (EU) 2024/2748 — inserted Art. 3(37), Art. 3(38) and a new Chapter IVa into Regulation 2023/1230 with effect from 29 May 2026 (internal market emergency mode). No change to Art. 51 or Art. 54.
- Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 — replaced Art. 47(6) with effect from 27 July 2026 (reflected in consolidated version 27/07/2026). No change to Art. 51 or Art. 54.
- Directive (EU) 2024/2749 — amended the Directive (not the Regulation); no change to the repeal date.
- Corrigenda R(01) (4.7.2023), R(02) (NL), R(03) (DE, SK), R(04) (SV) — only R(01) touches dates, and it is the source of the 20 January 2027 figure.

7. CITATION TABLE FOR THE FILE
| Point | Source | Text |
|---|---|---|
| Application date | Reg. 2023/1230, Art. 54(2) as corrected | 'It shall apply from 20 January 2027.' |
| Directive repealed | Reg. 2023/1230, Art. 51(2) as corrected | 'Directive 2006/42/EC is repealed with effect from 20 January 2027.' |
| Correction | OJ L 169, 4.7.2023, 35-36, items 5-7 | 14 January 2027 -> 20 January 2027; 13 July 2023 -> 19 July 2023 |
| Current consolidated version | CELEX 32023R1230, consolidation of 27/07/2026 | 'Date of effect: 20/01/2027; Application; See Art 54' |
| Corroboration (2026) | Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2026/2015, recital 14 and Art. 2 | repeal 'with effect from 20 January 2027' |
| Directive status today | EUR-Lex summary, CELEX 32006L0042 | 'repealed ... as of 20 January 2027'; 'remain applicable until 19 January 2027' |
| Transitional | Reg. 2023/1230, Art. 52 as corrected | legacy products placed on market before 20 January 2027; Chapter VI from 19 July 2023; certificates valid until expiry |

8. HOW TO STATE IT IN ONE SENTENCE
'Under Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 as corrected by the corrigendum of 4 July 2023 (OJ L 169, 4.7.2023, 35), the Regulation applies from 20 January 2027 and Directive 2006/42/EC is repealed with effect from that same date; as at 17 November 2026 the Directive is still in force and remains applicable until 19 January 2027, with products lawfully placed on the market before 20 January 2027 remaining freely available under Art. 52(1).'

# Dose limits for the lens of the eye under IAEA GSR Part 3 (2014) — answers and basis

## 1. Bottom line

| Ask | Question | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Occupational equivalent dose limit to the lens of the eye, workers over 18, GSR Part 3 (2014) | **20 mSv per year, averaged over 5 consecutive years (i.e. 100 mSv in 5 years), with no annual dose in a single year exceeding 50 mSv** |
| 2 | Annual lens limit that applied before the change described in the preface | **150 mSv in a year** |

Both figures are for *planned exposure situations* and for *occupational exposure of workers over the age of 18 years*.

## 2. Ask 1 — the current limit, in the standard's own structure

GSR Part 3 (2014), *Radiation Protection and Safety of Radiation Sources: International Basic Safety Standards*, Schedule III ("Dose Limits and Constraints for Public and Occupational Exposure"), section on dose limits for occupational exposure, sets the limits for occupational exposure of workers over 18 as:

- (a) an effective dose of **20 mSv per year averaged over 5 consecutive years (100 mSv in 5 years) and 50 mSv in any single year**;
- (b) an **equivalent dose to the lens of the eye of 20 mSv per year averaged over 5 consecutive years (100 mSv in 5 years) and 50 mSv in any single year**;
- (c) an equivalent dose to the extremities (hands and feet) or the skin of **500 mSv in a year**.

Additional restrictions apply to a female worker who has notified pregnancy or is breast-feeding (these do not change the numeric limit above).

The IAEA's own restatement of this schedule, in IAEA-TECDOC-1731, Annex I, which footnotes itself as "The dose limits are taken from Schedule III of GSR Part 3", reads verbatim:

> "For occupational exposure of workers over the age of 18 years, the dose limits are: … (b) An equivalent dose to the lens of the eye of 20 mSv per year averaged over 5 consecutive years (100 mSv in 5 years) and of 50 mSv in any single year;"

and, for apprentices aged 16–18 in training and students aged 16–18:

> "(b) An equivalent dose to the lens of the eye of 20 mSv in a year;"

**How the limit must be quoted.** The number 20 mSv is an *average over five consecutive years*, not a hard annual ceiling. The binding annual ceiling is 50 mSv in any single year, and the five-year total may not exceed 100 mSv. Quoting "20 mSv/a" alone without the averaging and the 50 mSv single-year cap misstates the standard; quoting "50 mSv/a" as *the* limit is also wrong — 50 mSv is a ceiling on a single year, not the limit itself. The IAEA's public-facing summary of the standard puts it the same way:

> "the IAEA General Safety Requirement Radiation Protection and Safety of Radiation Sources: International Basic Safety Standards (No. GSR Part 3) states that occupational exposure of the lens of the eye should be limited to an equivalent dose limit of 20 mSv per year, averaged over five years, with no annual dose in a single year exceeding 50 mSv."

## 3. Ask 2 — the pre-change limit and where the preface states it

The preface/foreword of GSR Part 3 records the change in exactly these terms (the foreword text, as reproduced verbatim in the IAEA publication IAEA-TECDOC-1731):

> "The equivalent dose limit for the lens of the eye for occupational exposure in planned exposure situations was reduced **from 150 mSv per year to 20 mSv per year**, averaged over defined periods of five years, with no annual dose in a single year exceeding 50 mSv. This reduction in the dose limit for the lens of the eye follows the recommendation of the International Commission on Radiological Protection (ICRP) in its statement on tissue reactions on 21 April 2011."

So the annual limit that had applied to the lens before the change was **150 mSv in a year**. That value is the occupational lens limit of the previous international basic safety standards (the 1996 edition, Safety Series No. 115), which in turn rested on ICRP Publication 60 (1990) and on a threshold-based (deterministic-effect) rationale for lens opacities.

Independent corroboration from IAEA material:

- IAEA-TECDOC-1731, main text: "For occupational exposure in planned exposure situations, the revised equivalent dose limits for the lens of the eye are 20 mSv in a year, averaged over 5 consecutive years (i.e. 100 mSv in 5 years), and 50 mSv in any single year. **These limits replace the previous limit on equivalent dose of 150 mSv in a year.**"
- IAEA conference contribution (2022): "In 2011 the ICRP published a statement on tissue reactions and has recommended reducing an equivalent dose limit for the lens of the eye **from 150 mSv per year to 20 mSv per year**, averaged over defined periods of five years, with no annual dose in a single year exceeding 50 mSv. In 2014 reduced annual occupational equivalent dose limit to the lens of the eye was adopted in the IAEA Safety Standards."

**Provenance note.** The reduction first entered the IAEA safety standards with the *Interim* edition of GSR Part 3 (approved September 2011, published November 2011); the 2014 edition is the final, approved version and carries the same numeric values unchanged. The preface's "before the change" baseline is therefore the 150 mSv/a value of the pre-2011 standards, not an earlier IAEA value of any other magnitude.

## 4. Adjacent numbers — read these correctly and do not substitute them

| Quantity | Value | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Occupational lens of eye, workers >18 (GSR Part 3, 2014) | 20 mSv/a averaged over 5 y; 100 mSv in 5 y; ≤50 mSv in any single year | The answer to ask 1 |
| Occupational lens of eye, before the change | 150 mSv in a year | The answer to ask 2 |
| Occupational effective dose, workers >18 | 20 mSv/a averaged over 5 y (100 mSv in 5 y); ≤50 mSv in any single year | Same averaging structure; not the lens limit |
| Occupational extremities (hands, feet) or skin | 500 mSv in a year | Not the lens limit |
| Lens of eye, apprentices/students aged 16–18 | 20 mSv in a year | Same number, but **no averaging**; the apprentices/students effective-dose limit is 6 mSv/a and skin/extremities 150 mSv/a — do not import the 150 into the adult lens answer |
| Lens of eye, members of the public | 15 mSv in a year | Public exposure, not occupational |

## 5. Consistency and arithmetic check of every value stated above

- 20 mSv/a × 5 consecutive years = 100 mSv in 5 years — exactly the five-year figure quoted; no contradiction.
- Single-year ceiling 50 mSv ≥ the 20 mSv/a average — consistent: the ceiling permits year-to-year variation above the average while the 5-year total stays ≤100 mSv.
- 150 mSv/a > 20 mSv/a — the change is correctly described as a *reduction*, by a factor of 7.5.
- Public lens limit 15 mSv/a < occupational 20 mSv/a — correct direction for public vs occupational.
- The 16–18 lens value (20 mSv in a year, unaveraged) is not numerically lower than the adult averaged value; the difference is the absence of averaging, which is stated explicitly rather than left implicit.
- No value in this deliverable exceeds or contradicts any bound set elsewhere in it.

## 6. Application notes and caveats

1. **Scope.** These are dose limits for occupational exposure in planned exposure situations. They apply to the sum of relevant doses from regulated practices; medical exposures of patients and natural background (with the specific radon provisions of GSR Part 3) are treated separately and are not counted against these limits.
2. **Units.** Both values are equivalent dose to a single tissue (the lens), expressed in millisieverts per year — not effective dose.
3. **Legal status.** GSR Part 3 is the international standard; national legislation may lag or differ (e.g. some states transposed the 20 mSv/a value only years later). Where the question is "what does GSR Part 3 say", the international values in §1 govern.
4. **Revisions/corrigenda.** No corrigendum or amendment to GSR Part 3 has altered these numeric values; the 2014 edition retains the figures adopted in the 2011 Interim edition.
5. **Citation precision.** The limits are located in GSR Part 3, Schedule III ("Dose Limits and Constraints for Public and Occupational Exposure"), in the section on dose limits for occupational exposure. Paragraph-level numbering inside Schedule III is not asserted here because it could not be verified from the sources consulted; if a downstream document requires a paragraph number, verify it against the printed Schedule III before citing, and otherwise cite "GSR Part 3, Schedule III" plus the requirement on dose limits, which is sufficient and accurate.

NIS2 INCIDENT NOTIFICATION DEADLINES — DIRECTIVE (EU) 2022/2555, ARTICLE 23(4)

BOTTOM LINE
- Trust service providers (TSPs): the incident notification for a significant incident that has an impact on the provision of their trust services must be submitted to the CSIRT or, where applicable, the competent authority without undue delay and in any event within 24 HOURS of becoming aware of the significant incident. Legal basis: Art. 23(4), second subparagraph, of Directive (EU) 2022/2555 — an express derogation from Art. 23(4), first subparagraph, point (b). Confirmed by the Commission's guidance published at OJ C 2023/328, para. 20.
- All other essential and important entities: the incident notification must be submitted to the CSIRT or, where applicable, the competent authority without undue delay and in any event within 72 HOURS of becoming aware of the significant incident. Legal basis: Art. 23(4), first subparagraph, point (b).

1. THE GENERAL STAGED REGIME (Art. 23(4), first subparagraph) — applies to essential and important entities other than TSPs in respect of trust-service incidents
| Stage | Trigger / clock start | Deadline | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) Early warning | becoming aware of the significant incident | without undue delay, and in any event within 24 hours | Art. 23(4)(a) |
| (b) Incident notification | becoming aware of the significant incident | without undue delay, and in any event within 72 hours | Art. 23(4)(b) |
| (c) Intermediate report | upon request of the CSIRT / competent authority | as specified in the request | Art. 23(4)(c) |
| (d) Final report | submission of the incident notification under (b) | not later than one month after that submission | Art. 23(4)(d) |
| (e) Ongoing incident | time of the final report | progress report at that time, final report within one month of handling | Art. 23(4)(e) |

2. THE TRUST SERVICE PROVIDER DEROGATION (Art. 23(4), second subparagraph)
Textual effect: 'By way of derogation from the first subparagraph, point (b), a trust service provider shall, with regard to significant incidents that have an impact on the provision of its trust services, notify the CSIRT or, where applicable, the competent authority, without undue delay and in any event within 24 hours of becoming aware of the significant incident.'

Four consequences to apply operationally:
(a) Scope of the derogation: it displaces only point (b), the 72-hour incident notification. It does not displace point (a), the early warning. A TSP therefore has a 24-hour early warning under (a) and a 24-hour incident notification under the second subparagraph — the two deadlines coincide. In practice TSPs commonly file a single notification at the 24-hour mark that satisfies both, but the two obligations remain legally distinct and the safe reading is to file within 24 hours.
(b) Scope ratione materiae: the 24-hour rule applies only to significant incidents 'that have an impact on the provision of its trust services'. A significant incident at a TSP that does not affect the provision of trust services falls back under the ordinary regime (24 h early warning / 72 h incident notification). Classification must therefore record expressly whether trust-service provision was affected.
(c) Clock start: 'becoming aware of the significant incident' — awareness of the significant incident, not awareness of the underlying event and not completion of the entity's own analysis. The 24-hour clock runs from that point.
(d) Downstream clock: the final report under point (d) is due 'not later than one month after the submission of the incident notification under point (b)'. For a TSP, that reference point is its own 24-hour notification; the one-month period is not measured from a 72-hour notification because no 72-hour notification is due from a TSP. Point (c) intermediate reports and point (e) ongoing-incident reports apply to TSPs unchanged.

3. WHERE THE NOTIFICATION GOES
- The addressee is 'the CSIRT or, where applicable, the competent authority' (Art. 23(1), first subparagraph, and Art. 23(4)). Which of the two receives it is fixed by the Member State's transposition and by its designation under Arts. 8(1) and 8(2).
- If the entity notifies the competent authority, the Member State must ensure that the competent authority forwards the notification to the CSIRT upon receipt (Art. 23(1), second subparagraph). The entity's obligation is discharged by notifying the designated addressee; the onward transmission is the Member State's duty, not a second filing by the entity.

4. WORKED TIMELINE (illustrative)
Aware at T0.
- TSP, trust services affected: early warning by T0+24h; incident notification by T0+24h; intermediate report if requested; final report by (date of the T0+24h notification) + 1 month.
- TSP, trust services not affected, or any other essential/important entity: early warning by T0+24h; incident notification by T0+72h; final report by (date of the T0+72h notification) + 1 month.

5. QUALIFICATIONS A COMPLIANCE FUNCTION SHOULD FLAG
- Legal basis used: the Directive as adopted (Directive (EU) 2022/2555), not any national transposition. Member States may not lengthen these maximum deadlines, but national law fixes the competent authority/CSIRT, the practical submission channel, the language, and any additional sectoral reporting. A jurisdiction-specific answer requires naming the Member State; the 24 h / 72 h figures above are the Directive's ceilings and are the correct baseline in every Member State.
- eIDAS interaction: Art. 42 of NIS2 amends Regulation (EU) No 910/2014. Trust service providers remain subject to eIDAS supervisory and breach-notification duties (including the 'without undue delay' notification of a breach of security or loss of integrity with significant adverse effect under Art. 19(2) of eIDAS, and the 24-hour notification to the supervisory body for qualified trust service providers where the breach concerns a qualified trust service). NIS2 Art. 23 notifications and eIDAS notifications run in parallel; compliance with one does not automatically satisfy the other. Sequencing should be planned so the NIS2 24-hour deadline is met independently.
- Definition: 'significant incident' is the Art. 23(3) test — (a) caused or capable of causing severe operational disruption of services or financial loss for the entity, or (b) affected or capable of affecting other natural or legal persons by causing considerable material or non-material damage.
- This answer addresses submission deadlines only, not the content of each report (Art. 23(4)(a)–(e)) or the voluntary/early-warning reporting channels under Art. 30.

question: X10
answer:
Answer: 56 hours.

Legal test
- Regulation (EC) No 561/2006, Article 4(i): a week is the period from 00:00 on Monday to 24:00 on Sunday.
- Article 6(2): weekly driving time shall not exceed 56 hours.
- Article 6(3): total accumulated driving time during any two consecutive weeks shall not exceed 90 hours.

Calculation
Let x be the driving time in the week following the 30-hour week.
1. Weekly limit: x ≤ 56 hours.
2. Two-week limit: 30 + x ≤ 90, so x ≤ 60 hours.
Binding cap: x ≤ min(56, 60) = 56 hours.

Verification
- Weekly limit: 56 ≤ 56. Satisfied exactly.
- Two-week limit: 30 + 56 = 86 ≤ 90. Satisfied with 4 hours of fortnightly headroom unused.
- The fortnightly headroom of 60 hours cannot be used because the 56-hour weekly cap binds first.

Attainability under the daily driving limits
Article 6(1) permits 9 hours of daily driving, extendable to 10 hours not more than twice in the week. A total of 56 hours is reachable as 4 days × 9 hours + 2 days × 10 hours = 56 hours over six driving days, with the seventh day free of driving. This shows that 56 hours is not contradicted by the daily driving limits, provided daily and weekly rest, breaks and tachograph recording obligations are met. Rest or working-time constraints may reduce what is achievable in practice; they do not increase the 56-hour weekly driving cap.

Scope and caveats
- The result is the maximum driving time under the EU drivers' hours rules. It is an upper bound, not an entitlement or a requirement to drive 56 hours.
- Night work, ferry or multi-manning provisions do not change the 56-hour weekly or 90-hour fortnightly driving maxima.
- If the driver is not actually subject to Regulation (EC) No 561/2006 because a national exemption or other regime applies, different limits may apply and this answer would need to be reassessed.
- The two-week window that constrains the following week is the 30-hour week plus the following week. A later two-week window involving the following week and the week after cannot be assessed without data for the week after, but it does not reduce the following week's own maximum below 56 hours because the week after can be planned within the remaining fortnightly headroom.

# Legal note: employee-count threshold for mandatory DPO appointment under the GDPR

## 1. Direct answer

**The GDPR (Regulation (EU) 2016/679) sets no employee-count threshold at all.** There is no number of employees — 20, 250, or any other — at which a controller or processor becomes obliged to designate a data protection officer under the Regulation itself. Article 37(1) contains three qualitative triggers and none of them refers to headcount, turnover, or establishment size. Recital 97 likewise contains no headcount.

The figure that is usually behind this question is **20**, and it is real — but it comes from **German national law, § 38(1) sentence 1 of the Bundesdatenschutzgesetz (BDSG)**, enacted under the opening that Article 37(4) GDPR leaves to Member States. It binds non-public bodies established in Germany. It is not a GDPR requirement, it does not apply EU-wide, and it is not even a pure total-headcount test (see §4 below).

## 2. What Article 37 actually requires

Article 37(1) GDPR, verbatim in the operative part: the controller and the processor shall designate a DPO in any case where:

| # | Trigger | Text of Art. 37(1) | Headcount relevant? |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) | Public authority or body | "the processing is carried out by a public authority or body, except for courts acting in their judicial capacity" | No |
| (b) | Regular and systematic monitoring at large scale as a core activity | "the core activities of the controller or the processor consist of processing operations which, by virtue of their nature, their scope and/or their purposes, require regular and systematic monitoring of data subjects on a large scale" | No |
| (c) | Large-scale Art. 9 / Art. 10 data as a core activity | "the core activities of the controller or the processor consist of processing on a large scale of special categories of data pursuant to Article 9 and personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences referred to in Article 10" | No |
| — | Required by Union or Member State law | Art. 37(4): "In cases other than those referred to in paragraph 1, the controller or processor ... may or, where required by Union or Member State law shall, designate a data protection officer" | Depends on the national law |
| — | Voluntary | Art. 37(4) "may" | Not applicable |

Supporting provisions relevant to the assessment:

- **Art. 37(2)** — a group of undertakings may appoint a single DPO provided that a DPO is easily accessible from each establishment. Group size is therefore a design question, not a trigger.
- **Art. 37(3)** — a public authority or body may designate a single DPO for several authorities/bodies, taking account of organisational structure and size.
- **Art. 37(5)–(7)** — the DPO is designated on professional qualities and expert knowledge of data protection law and practice; the DPO **may be a staff member or may fulfil the tasks on the basis of a service contract** (i.e. an external DPO is fully compliant); contact details must be published and communicated to the supervisory authority.
- **Recital 97** — repeats the same three triggers in prose (public authority; private-sector core activities requiring regular and systematic monitoring on a large scale; large-scale special-category and criminal-offence data) and confirms the DPO may be a staff member or a service contractor. It says nothing about employee numbers.
- **Arts. 38–39** — position (independence, no instructions, no dismissal or penalty, direct reporting to the highest management level, no conflict of interests) and tasks (advice, monitoring, DPIA advice, cooperation with the supervisory authority, awareness-raising, training, records).

**Consequence of the drafting:** whether a DPO is mandatory is a *processing-based* test, not a *size-based* test. A three-person start-up whose core activity is large-scale processing of health data must appoint a DPO. A 5,000-employee logistics company whose core activity is moving freight, with only ancillary HR and payroll processing, is not caught by Art. 37(1)(b) or (c) — though it may be caught by Art. 37(1)(a) if it is a public body, or by national law under Art. 37(4).

## 3. How "large scale" and "core activities" are assessed (WP29/EDPB)

There is no numeric definition of "large scale" in the Regulation. The reference guidance is the Article 29 Working Party **Guidelines on Data Protection Officers (WP243 rev.01)**, adopted 13 December 2016, last revised 5 April 2017, and endorsed by the EDPB.

- **Core activities** = the key operations necessary to achieve the controller's or processor's goals. Ancillary processing (e.g. ordinary HR administration, payroll, standard office IT) is not a core activity. WP29's illustration: a hospital's core activity is the provision of healthcare, so its patient-data processing is core; a pharmaceutical company's clinical-trial data processing is core; a private security firm whose business is surveillance of clients' premises has monitoring as a core activity, whereas a shopping centre that runs ancillary CCTV is in a different position.
- **Large scale** is assessed on four factors, none of which is headcount of the controller:
  1. the **number of data subjects** concerned, either as a specific number or as a proportion of the relevant population;
  2. the **volume of data and/or the range of different data items** processed;
  3. the **duration, or permanence**, of the processing activity;
  4. the **geographical extent** of the processing activity.
- WP29 expressly notes that processing by an individual physician, an individual lawyer or a small law firm is not large-scale processing of special categories.

## 4. The number people actually mean: Germany, § 38 BDSG

The German provision (non-official translation of § 38(1) BDSG):

> "(1) Supplementary to Article 37(1)(b) and (c) of Regulation (EU) 2016/679, the controller and the processor shall designate a data protection officer **if they regularly employ at least 20 persons constantly engaged in the automated processing of personal data**. If the controller or the processor carries out processing operations which are subject to a data protection impact assessment pursuant to Article 35 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679, or if they process personal data on a commercial basis for the purpose of transmission, anonymised transmission or for the purposes of market or opinion research, they shall designate a data protection officer **irrespective of the number of persons engaged in the processing**."

Key qualifications that are routinely lost when "20" is quoted:

1. **It is national law, not GDPR.** It applies to *nichtöffentliche Stellen* — non-public bodies — within Germany's territorial scope. Public bodies in Germany fall under separate provisions (§ 5 BDSG) and Art. 37(1)(a).
2. **It is not total headcount.** The count is of persons *constantly engaged in automated processing of personal data* ("ständig mit der automatisierten Verarbeitung personenbezogener Daten beschäftigen"), and it must be satisfied *as a rule* ("in der Regel"). A 200-employee manufacturer with 12 staff touching automated personal-data processing may fall below it; a 25-person analytics company will exceed it.
3. **Headcount is irrelevant if the second sentence applies.** Processing subject to a DPIA under Art. 35, or commercial processing for transmission/anonymised transmission/market or opinion research, triggers the DPO duty regardless of the number of persons.
4. **Part-time counting is not codified in § 38.** The former § 4f BDSG contained an express pro-rata rule for part-time staff (0.5 below 20 hours, 0.75 up to 30 hours). That rule was not carried into § 38. Practice varies; some supervisory authorities apply pro-rata counting by analogy, others count persons. This point should be confirmed with German counsel against the current supervisory-authority guidance before it is relied on.
5. **Verify currency.** § 38 has been the subject of reform debate in Germany; the version cited here is the one fetched from gesetze-im-internet.de. Any live decision should be re-checked against the version in force at the time.

## 5. Other jurisdictions

- **UK GDPR** — Art. 37 UK GDPR replicates the three EU triggers; there is no general employee-count threshold in the UK GDPR or the Data Protection Act 2018. (The UK regime has its own public-authority and sectoral obligations, which should be checked separately for public bodies.)
- **Other EU/EEA Member States** — Art. 37(4) permits Member States to require a DPO in additional cases, and several have done so, sometimes with headcount-linked or list-based rules and sometimes by sector. **Do not generalise the German 20-person rule to any other Member State.** Where the entity is established, or where Art. 3(2) applies, the law of each relevant Member State must be checked individually. This memo does not substitute for that check.

## 6. Decision procedure (apply in order)

```
DPO_MANDATORY(entity E):
  1. Is E a public authority or body (excluding courts in their judicial capacity)?
       YES -> DPO mandatory under Art. 37(1)(a). STOP.
  2. Identify E's CORE activities (key operations necessary to achieve E's goals;
     exclude ancillary HR, payroll, office IT).
  3. Do those core activities consist of processing operations that, by nature,
     scope and/or purposes, REQUIRE REGULAR AND SYSTEMATIC MONITORING of data
     subjects ON A LARGE SCALE?
       Apply the four WP243 factors: number of data subjects; volume/range of data;
       duration/permanence; geographical extent.
       YES -> DPO mandatory under Art. 37(1)(b). STOP.
  4. Do those core activities consist of processing ON A LARGE SCALE of Art. 9
     special-category data or Art. 10 criminal-conviction/offence data?
       YES -> DPO mandatory under Art. 37(1)(c). STOP.
  5. Does the law of any Member State in which E is established (or to which
     Art. 3(2) extends E's processing) require a DPO under Art. 37(4)?
       For Germany (non-public bodies): does E regularly employ >= 20 persons
       constantly engaged in automated processing of personal data, OR carry out
       Art. 35 DPIA-required processing, OR process personal data commercially
       for transmission / anonymised transmission / market or opinion research?
       YES (any limb) -> DPO mandatory under national law. STOP.
  6. Otherwise: no mandatory DPO. Consider VOLUNTARY designation under
     Art. 37(4) — but note that once designated, Arts. 37-39 apply in full
     (independence, no dismissal/penalty, no conflict of interests, publication
     of contact details). A voluntary appointment is a governance decision, not
     a free option.

  Throughout: E's EMPLOYEE COUNT is not a GDPR criterion. Staff numbers are
  relevant only where a national rule (e.g. § 38 BDSG) uses them, and even then
  the relevant count may be staff engaged in automated processing, not total
  headcount.
```

## 7. Consequences of getting it wrong

- **Failure to designate a required DPO** is an infringement of an obligation under Arts. 25–39 and therefore falls within **Art. 83(4)(a)**: administrative fines of up to **EUR 10,000,000**, or, for an undertaking, **2% of total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher**.
- Supervisory authorities may also order the controller or processor to bring processing into compliance, and may impose a temporary or definitive limitation or ban (Art. 58(2)).
- **Over-appointment is not free.** Designating a DPO voluntarily under Art. 37(4) brings Arts. 37–39 fully into play: independence, prohibition on instructions, protection from dismissal and penalty, direct reporting to the highest management level, the Art. 38(6) conflict-of-interests constraint (which can disqualify e.g. a Head of HR, IT, or Compliance from the role), publication of contact details, and communication to the supervisory authority. The appointment should therefore be made deliberately, not defensively.
- The DPO's function is advisory and monitoring (Art. 39); the DPO does not absorb the controller's own accountability obligations under Art. 5(2).

## 8. Limits of this note

- No Member State law other than Germany's § 38 BDSG has been examined here. The question as posed cannot be answered for a specific entity without knowing its establishment(s), its sector, and its processing operations.
- The "large scale" determination is fact-specific; WP243 gives factors, not a safe-harbour number.
- The part-time counting question under § 38 BDSG (point 4 in §4 above) is genuinely unsettled on the face of the statute and requires German-law confirmation.
- This is a legal-analysis summary for engineering and compliance planning, not a formal legal opinion or advice on a specific entity's position.

# 4.1.1 Parsing — vendor questionnaire answer (WCAG 2.x, December 2024 publication, target Level AA)

## 0. First: the premise needs one correction before the answer is safe

The phrase "the W3C web content accessibility Recommendation published in December 2024" is **not unique**. On **12 December 2024** W3C published updates to **two** WCAG 2.x Recommendations, and 4.1.1 has a different status in each:

| Document | December 2024 publication | 4.1.1 status | Must a page pass it for Level AA? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **WCAG 2.2** | update published 12 December 2024 (WAI FAQ: *"On 12 December 2024, we published an update to WCAG 2.2."*); latest version `https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/` | **Removed** — not a success criterion in 2.2 | **No** |
| **WCAG 2.1** | dated Recommendation `https://www.w3.org/TR/2024/REC-WCAG21-20241212/` | **Still a Level A success criterion**, carrying an informative note calling it obsolete | **Yes** |
| (WCAG 2.0, 11 Dec 2008 — not a December 2024 publication) | — | Level A success criterion | Yes |

**Selection rule to apply to the questionnaire:**
1. If the questionnaire cites **WCAG 2.2**, `/TR/WCAG22/`, or a 2024-dated 2.2 REC URL → use the **2.2 branch (§1 below). Answer: NO.**
2. If it cites **WCAG 2.1**, `/TR/WCAG21/`, or `REC-WCAG21-20241212` → use the **2.1 branch (§3 below). Answer: YES.**
3. If it cites only "December 2024" with no version → answer on the 2.2 branch (2.2 is the current Recommendation and the edition in which 4.1.1's removal is the December-2024-relevant fact), **and** state the version you answered against in the response, e.g. *"Answered against WCAG 2.2 (W3C Recommendation, 12 December 2024 update). If your reference is WCAG 2.1 (REC-WCAG21-20241212), see the note in the same cell."* This removes the ambiguity from the record rather than silently guessing.

Everything below assumes the 2.2 branch unless labelled otherwise.

---

## 1. Ask 1 — Verdict: **NO**, a page does not have to pass 4.1.1 to conform to WCAG 2.2 at Level AA

4.1.1 is **not a success criterion in WCAG 2.2**. Conformance is defined entirely as satisfying *the success criteria that exist in that document*, so a criterion that is not in the document cannot be a condition of conformance. It can be neither passed nor failed.

**Normative chain (each step quoted from the Recommendation):**

1. **§5.2 Conformance Requirements** — *"In order for a web page to conform to WCAG 2.2, all of the following conformance requirements must be satisfied:"*
2. **§5.2.1 Conformance Level** — *"For Level AA conformance, the web page satisfies all the Level A and Level AA success criteria, or a Level AA conforming alternate version is provided."*
3. **The Level A / Level AA set in WCAG 2.2 does not contain 4.1.1.** Guideline 4.1 Compatible contains 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (A) and 4.1.3 Status Messages (AA). 4.1.1 Parsing was removed in WCAG 2.2.
4. **Therefore:** Level AA conformance under WCAG 2.2 = all Level A and Level AA success criteria *of WCAG 2.2*, which excludes 4.1.1. No obligation attaches to 4.1.1.

**Corroboration from W3C's own accompanying material:**

- WAI, *WCAG 2 Overview*: *"The WCAG 2 requirements (success criteria) are the same in later versions. For example, the success criteria in WCAG 2.1 are not changed in WCAG 2.2. Later versions add new success criteria, and do not change existing success criteria. One exception is 4.1.1 Parsing noted below."*
- Understanding SC 4.1.1, page title: **"Parsing (Obsolete and removed)"**; body: *"This criterion has been removed from WCAG 2.2."*
- Technique F77 (obsolete failure technique): *"This failure relates to 4.1.1 Parsing, which was removed as of WCAG 2.2."*
- WAI WCAG FAQ: *"(Using tools that assess parsing errors and fixing parsing issues may still be useful — it's just not required for accessibility.)"*

**What this means for the questionnaire's pass/fail field:**

- **Do not answer "Fail."** Reporting Fail asserts non-conformance to a requirement that does not exist in the cited document, and would misrepresent the page/site.
- **Do not answer a bare "Pass" either.** It implies an evaluation was performed against a live criterion and can be read as a claim of parsing remediation work that WCAG 2.2 does not ask for.
- **Answer: "N/A — criterion removed in WCAG 2.2"** (equivalently "Not applicable / obsolete"), with the one-line citation. If the form's control only permits Pass/Fail, select **Pass** and put the N/A explanation plus citation in the comments field, so the record shows the criterion was considered and is inapplicable rather than silently skipped.

**Do not over-read the removal.** Duplicate `id` values and broken markup still cause real failures *where they break something else* — e.g. a duplicated `id` that breaks a `for`/`id` label association or an `aria-labelledby` reference is a **1.3.1 Info and Relationships** and/or **4.1.2 Name, Role, Value** failure under 2.2. Keep validating markup; just do not report the result as a 4.1.1 result.

**Per-page vs site:** WCAG 2.2's conformance model is per **web page** (§5.2.1 read with §5.2.2 Full pages); a site-level claim is a claim about a set of pages, not a separate unit. The verdict above holds identically at page level and therefore at site level.

---

## 2. Ask 2 — What the document says is the reason

**Reason code: `AT_NO_LONGER_PARSES_HTML`** — the criterion was removed because assistive technology no longer needs to parse HTML directly; the parsing problems it targeted either no longer occur or are caught by other criteria.

**Attribution matters here, so it is stated precisely:** the *removal* is normative (4.1.1 is absent from WCAG 2.2's success criteria, and §5.2.1 conditions conformance on that set). The *rationale* is not restated in WCAG 2.2's conformance section; W3C states it in the note carried with the criterion and in the accompanying Understanding document, which is explicitly labelled informative (*"Informative explanations, not required to meet WCAG"*). Quote it as W3C's stated rationale, not as a normative conformance requirement.

**Verbatim — note attached to SC 4.1.1 (Understanding SC 4.1.1, "Parsing (Obsolete and removed)"):**

> "This criterion was originally adopted to address problems that assistive technology had directly parsing HTML. Assistive technology no longer has any need to directly parse HTML. Consequently, these problems either no longer exist or are addressed by other criteria. This criterion no longer has utility and is removed."

**Verbatim — Intent section, same page:**

> "This criterion has been removed from WCAG 2.2. The intent of this success criterion was to ensure that user agents, including assistive technologies, can accurately interpret and parse content. Since WCAG 2.0 was published, the specifications (such as HTML) and browsers have improved their handling of parsing errors. It is also the case that assistive technology used to do their own parsing of markup, but now rely on the browser. For that reason this success criterion has been removed. Many issues that would have failed this criterion will fail Info and Relationships or Name, Role, Value. Other issues are excepted by the 'except where the specification allow these features' part of the criterion."

**Decomposition of the stated reason (use whichever level of detail the questionnaire wants):**

| # | Stated reason | Source phrasing |
|---|---|---|
| R1 | Assistive technology no longer parses HTML itself; it relies on the browser | "Assistive technology no longer has any need to directly parse HTML" / "now rely on the browser" |
| R2 | Since WCAG 2.0, HTML and browsers handle parsing errors far better | "the specifications (such as HTML) and browsers have improved their handling of parsing errors" |
| R3 | The problems it targeted either no longer exist or are covered by other criteria (1.3.1 Info and Relationships; 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value), or are excepted by "except where the specifications allow these features" | "these problems either no longer exist or are addressed by other criteria" / "Many issues that would have failed this criterion will fail Info and Relationships or Name, Role, Value" |
| R4 | Conclusion: no remaining utility → removed | "This criterion no longer has utility and is removed." |

---

## 3. Branch: if the questionnaire means WCAG 2.1 (REC-WCAG21-20241212) — verdict **YES**

WCAG 2.1's own conformance text is unchanged in structure: *"In order for a Web page to conform to WCAG 2.1, all of the following conformance requirements must be satisfied: … For Level AA conformance, the Web page satisfies all the Level A and Level AA Success Criteria, or a Level AA conforming alternate version is provided."* 4.1.1 Parsing **remains a normative Level A success criterion in WCAG 2.1**, including in the 12 December 2024 dated Recommendation (that revision's stated changes are "minor formatting and editorial changes listed in the WCAG 2.1 Change Log"). Therefore, at Level AA against WCAG 2.1, a page **must** satisfy 4.1.1, notwithstanding the informative note added in the 21 September 2023 revision calling it obsolete.

Answer in that case: **"Pass/Fail applies — 4.1.1 is still a Level A success criterion in WCAG 2.1 (REC-WCAG21-20241212). Note: the criterion carries an informative note from W3C that it is obsolete and has been removed in WCAG 2.2; results should be read with that in mind."** Report the measured result (e.g. duplicate `id` values → Fail under 2.1) and add the obsolescence note so the record is not misleading.

*Confirm before quoting:* open §4.1.1 of `https://www.w3.org/TR/2024/REC-WCAG21-20241212/` and verify the SC text and its note are present in that dated revision (the note's presence there follows from the 2023-09-21 addition plus the 2024-12-12 editorial-only change, but quote from the dated REC itself, not from the latest-version URL).

---

## 4. Copy-paste response text for the questionnaire

**4.1.1 Parsing (Level A) — result field:**

```
N/A — Removed in WCAG 2.2.
```

**Justification / comments field:**

```
Success Criterion 4.1.1 Parsing was removed in WCAG 2.2. It is not a success criterion in
that Recommendation, so it is not part of the Level A / Level AA set on which conformance
depends (WCAG 2.2 §5.2.1: "For Level AA conformance, the web page satisfies all the Level A
and Level AA success criteria..."). The criterion therefore cannot be passed or failed under
WCAG 2.2, and is reported as Not Applicable rather than Pass or Fail.

W3C's stated reason (note carried with 4.1.1; elaborated in Understanding SC 4.1.1, which is
informative): "This criterion was originally adopted to address problems that assistive
technology had directly parsing HTML. Assistive technology no longer has any need to directly
parse HTML. Consequently, these problems either no longer exist or are addressed by other
criteria. This criterion no longer has utility and is removed."

We continue to validate markup: parsing defects that actually break relationships or exposed
name/role/value are evaluated and reported under 1.3.1 Info and Relationships and 4.1.2 Name,
Role, Value, which remain Level A requirements in WCAG 2.2.

Reference: WCAG 2.2, W3C Recommendation (update published 12 December 2024),
https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/ ; Understanding SC 4.1.1 "Parsing (Obsolete and removed)".
```

**If the form rejects free text and forces Pass/Fail:** select **Pass**, and place the block above in the comments field verbatim. A bare Fail is incorrect; a bare Pass without the note misstates what was evaluated.

**If the questionnaire's citation is WCAG 2.1 (REC-WCAG21-20241212):** replace the first paragraph with:

```
SC 4.1.1 Parsing is a Level A success criterion in WCAG 2.1 (W3C Recommendation,
12 December 2024 revision) and is therefore required for Level AA conformance to that
document. Result: [Pass/Fail + evidence]. Note: W3C has annotated this criterion as obsolete;
it was removed in WCAG 2.2.
```

---

## 5. Verification procedure (reproducible; do this before the response is filed)

1. Open `https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/`; confirm the Status of This Document / header shows a **W3C Recommendation** and the **12 December 2024** date. Record the exact dated-URL form used by your QA process (the dated 2.2 URL was not independently fetched in this research — take it from the document header, do not guess it).
2. Go to **§4.1 Compatible**; confirm the success criteria present are **4.1.2 Name, Role, Value** and **4.1.3 Status Messages**, and that **no 4.1.1 success criterion** is listed (at most a removal note).
3. Go to **§5.2.1 Conformance Level**; confirm the Level AA sentence reads "all the Level A and Level AA success criteria".
4. Open the 4.1.1 Understanding page; confirm the title reads **"Parsing (Obsolete and removed)"** and copy the note and Intent text exactly as quoted in §2 (watch for curly quotes / line-wrap artifacts).
5. Open F77; confirm the "Obsolete" banner and the sentence "…removed as of WCAG 2.2."
6. For the 2.1 branch, open `https://www.w3.org/TR/2024/REC-WCAG21-20241212/`, go to §4.1.1, and confirm the SC text plus its informative note are present in that dated revision.
7. Attach to the questionnaire record: document title, version, dated URL, retrieval date, and the verbatim quote used. If your QA process requires page hashes, hash the fetched pages at retrieval time.

---

## 6. Pitfalls that produce a wrong answer on this form

1. **Answering "Fail" because the audit found duplicate `id`s or unclosed tags.** Under WCAG 2.2 that is not a 4.1.1 failure — the criterion does not exist. Re-test the finding's actual impact and report it under 1.3.1 / 4.1.2 if it breaks assistive-technology exposure.
2. **Answering a bare "Pass".** Implies an evaluation of a live criterion and can be read as a remediation claim. Use "N/A — removed", with "Pass" only if the control is binary, plus the note.
3. **Treating the Understanding document as normative.** Its own banner says: *"Informative explanations, not required to meet WCAG."* The conformance obligation comes from WCAG 2.2 §5.2.1 and the SC set; the rationale comes from the note/Understanding text.
4. **Assuming "December 2024 Recommendation" identifies one document.** It does not — 2.1 and 2.2 were both updated on 12 December 2024. Always state which edition you answered against.
5. **Citing `/TR/WCAG21/` while the questionnaire means 2.2, or vice versa.** `/TR/WCAG21/` is the *latest* 2.1 (still contains 4.1.1); `/TR/WCAG22/` is 2.2 (does not).
6. **Concluding "markup quality no longer matters."** W3C's own FAQ says fixing parsing issues "may still be useful — it's just not required for accessibility"; residual defects are absorbed by 1.3.1 and 4.1.2.
7. **Assuming the 2.2 answer applies to a procurement pinned to WCAG 2.1.** If the contract, regulation, or VPAT template references WCAG 2.1 (directly or via a standard that pins 2.1), the 2.1 branch in §3 governs and 4.1.1 must be evaluated.

---

## 7. Bottom line for the two questionnaire fields

- **Must a page pass 4.1.1 to conform to WCAG 2.2 (December 2024 update) at Level AA? → No.** 4.1.1 is removed in WCAG 2.2; conformance at AA is defined by the Level A and Level AA success criteria that exist in that document, and 4.1.1 is not one of them. Report **N/A — removed**, not Fail.
- **What does the document say is the reason? → `AT_NO_LONGER_PARSES_HTML`:** *"Assistive technology no longer has any need to directly parse HTML. Consequently, these problems either no longer exist or are addressed by other criteria. This criterion no longer has utility and is removed."* (W3C note on 4.1.1; expanded in Understanding SC 4.1.1, which is informative — the removal itself is normative.)
- **If the cited document is WCAG 2.1 (REC-WCAG21-20241212): → Yes, 4.1.1 is still required at Level A and therefore for AA, with an informative obsolescence note.**

# AC-7 (Unsuccessful Logon Attempts) — what Rev. 5 actually requires

## Answer

**NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, AC-7, requires no specific number of attempts, no specific time window, and no specific lockout duration.** All three are *Assignment* (and, for the response, *Selection*) operations that the organization must fill in. The control is a requirement to *have* a limit and *have* an automatic response — not a requirement to use particular figures.

Verbatim control text (from the NIST CSRC Rev. 5 controls export, sha256 6fc1c2414396):

> **AC-7 Unsuccessful Logon Attempts**
> a. Enforce a limit of [Assignment: organization-defined number] consecutive invalid logon attempts by a user during a [Assignment: organization-defined time period]; and
> b. Automatically [Selection (one or more): lock the account or node for an [Assignment: organization-defined time period]; lock the account or node until released by an administrator; delay next logon prompt per [Assignment: organization-defined delay algorithm]; notify system administrator; take other [Assignment: organization-defined action].

So the three questions map to the control like this:

| Ask | What AC-7 says | Who supplies the value |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Number of consecutive invalid logon attempts | `[Assignment: organization-defined number]` | The organization, documented in its security plan / policy |
| 2. Time period within which they must occur | `[Assignment: organization-defined time period]` | The organization |
| 3. Lockout duration | `[Assignment: organization-defined time period]` — **only if** the organization selects the “lock for a period” option; the other four selections are valid alternatives | The organization |

Note on ask 3 in particular: AC-7b is a *Selection*, not a single mandatory response. An organization that selects “lock the account until released by an administrator” has **no** lockout duration at all. There is therefore no single correct answer to ask 3 even in principle — the control permits five distinct responses, only one of which has a duration.

## Why you may have seen “3 attempts / 15 minutes / 15-minute lockout”

The figure 3-15-15 circulates widely and is often attributed to NIST SP 800-53. It is **not in AC-7 and not in AC-7’s enhancements.** The Rev. 5 enhancements are written the same parameterized way — e.g. AC-7(1) Automatic Account Lockout likewise takes an organization-defined number of consecutive invalid attempts rather than a constant, and AC-7(4) Use of Alternate Authentication Factor (quoted from the same source) is entirely `[Assignment: organization-defined …]`:

> AC-7(4) … (a) Allow the use of [Assignment: organization-defined authentication factors] that are different from the primary authentication factors after the number of organization-defined consecutive invalid logon attempts have been exceeded; and (b) Enforce a limit of [Assignment: organization-defined number] consecutive invalid logon attempts through use of the alternative factors by a user during a [Assignment: organization-defined time period].

The 3-15-15 figure is an *organizational/vendor* choice (it appears in DISA STIGs and in many agency security plans and commercial defaults). It is a defensible choice, but citing AC-7 for it is a misattribution. To my knowledge, SP 800-53B scopes *which* controls and enhancements apply at each impact baselining (AC-7 is in the low baselining and above) but does not substitute numbers for AC-7’s assignments — **verify this against the current 800-53B before relying on it**, since baselining overlays are revised independently of the control catalog.

## What the organization must actually do

1. **Assign and document** the three parameters (plus the AC-7b selection) in the system security plan and in the organization’s policy. That documented value — not a NIST constant — is what an assessor tests against under SP 800-53A (AC-07a / AC-07b).
2. **Pick a response that fits the threat model.** The AC-7(4) discussion text (quoted above) makes the trade-off explicit: alternate factors “support the objective of availability and allow a user who has inadvertently been locked out” to recover — i.e. lockout is a denial-of-service vector against a known username, which is why AC-7b offers delay algorithms and administrator release as alternatives to hard lockout.
3. **Do not treat “no NIST number” as “no requirement.”** AC-7 is a real, assessable control: an account with unlimited attempts, or with a limit but no automatic response, fails regardless of which numbers are chosen.

## Implementation: making the three parameters configurable (backend)

Because the values are organizational inputs, the correct engineering pattern is a policy object, not hard-coded constants. Minimal schema:

```json
{
  "policy_id": "ac7-default",
  "max_consecutive_invalid_attempts": 3,          // AC-7a [Assignment] — ORG CHOICE, not NIST
  "attempt_window_seconds": 900,                   // AC-7a [Assignment] — 15 min, ORG CHOICE
  "counting_scope": "per_user_id",                 // or per_user_id+source_ip
  "response": {
    "type": "lock_for_period",                     // lock_for_period | admin_release | delay | notify_only | custom
    "lockout_seconds": 900,                        // AC-7b [Assignment] — only when type = lock_for_period
    "delay_algorithm": null,                        // e.g. exponential backoff parameters
    "notify_admin": true,
    "alternate_factors_allowed": ["fido2", "recovery_code"]   // AC-7(4)
  },
  "reset_counter_on_success": true,
  "window_semantics": "sliding"
}
```

The numbers above are an **example organizational choice**; they are not derived from, and must not be cited to, AC-7.

State machine (pseudocode, transactionally safe):

```
function on_logon_attempt(user_id, factor, source):
  tx:
    rec = SELECT ... FROM logon_state WHERE user_id = ? FOR UPDATE
    if rec.locked_until is not null and now < rec.locked_until:
        return DENY_LOCKED(rec.locked_until)          // AC-7b
    if rec.locked_until is not null and now >= rec.locked_until:
        rec.locked_until = null; rec.failures = []     // automatic release after the assigned period

    if verify(factor):
        rec.failures = []                              // consecurity is broken by success
        return ALLOW

    cutoff = now - policy.attempt_window_seconds
    rec.failures = [t for t in rec.failures if t > cutoff] + [now]   // sliding window
    if len(rec.failures) >= policy.max_consecutive_invalid_attempts:
        apply(policy.response) -> rec.locked_until = now + lockout_seconds (or null if admin_release)
        emit audit_event(AC7_LOCKOUT, user_id, count=len(rec.failures))
    return DENY_INVALID(remaining = policy.max - len(rec.failures))
```

Implementation points that are easy to get wrong:

- **Consectiveness is window-scoped, not lifetime.** If the assigned window is T, count only failures with timestamp > now − T; otherwise a slow brute force evades the limit.
- **Reset on success** is implied by “consecurity” and should be an explicit policy flag, not an accident of implementation.
- **Row-level locking** on the counter (`FOR UPDATE` / atomic increment) — otherwise parallel attempts defeat the limit.
- **Emit an audit event** for both the lockout and the automatic release; AC-7 is assessed on evidence.
- **Admin release path** and **alternate-factor path** (AC-7(4)) must both exist if the org selects them, or the control cannot be met as written.
- **Do not log the submitted password** when recording a failure; log the user identifier, source, timestamp, and count only.

## Bottom line for the three asks

AC-7 answers “you must have a limit, a window, and an automatic response — define them.” It does not answer “3 / 15 / 15,” and any document claiming NIST mandates those figures for AC-7 is misattributing organizational or vendor guidance.

question: X22
answer:
Answer for a current mainline Linux kernel on the 0-200 swappiness scale:

1. Accepted range: 0-200 inclusive. `vm.swappiness` is an integer sysctl; the kernel bounds it at 0 and 200, so writes below 0 or above 200 are rejected with EINVAL. On older kernels that predate the 0-200 scale, 133 may be above that kernel's accepted maximum; use the maximum documented for that kernel.

2. Default: 60. This is the upstream kernel default. Verify with `cat /proc/sys/vm/swappiness` or `sysctl -n vm.swappiness`. Distributions may override it, but 60 is the upstream default.

3. Value for a swap device whose random IO averages 2x faster than filesystem IO: 133. The kernel documentation gives this exact example:

   "For in-memory swap, like zram or zswap, as well as hybrid setups that have swap on faster devices than the filesystem, values beyond 100 can be considered. For example, if the random IO against the swap device is on average 2x faster than IO from the filesystem, swappiness should be 133 (x + 2x = 200, 2x = 133.33)."

   The model is: at 100 the VM assumes equal IO cost between swap-backed and file-backed pages; lower values mean swap IO is more expensive; higher values mean swap IO is cheaper. Since the swap device is 2x faster, 133 is the documented integer setting, derived from 133.33 rounded down. It is within the accepted 0-200 range and above 100, as the documentation recommends for zram/zswap or faster swap devices.

Apply it:

```
sysctl -w vm.swappiness=133
```

Persist it:

```
# /etc/sysctl.d/99-swappiness.conf
vm.swappiness = 133
```

```
sysctl --system
```

Verify:

```
sysctl -n vm.swappiness   # should print 133
```

Caveats:
- 133 is the correct starting point for the stated 2x cost ratio, not a universal zram setting. If zram's advantage is much larger than 2x, higher values may test better; if CPU compression/decompression cost is material, the effective advantage is smaller and a lower value may be better.
- The kernel documentation notes that filesystem IO under memory pressure tends to be more efficient than swap's random IO, and that the optimal value is workload-dependent. Validate under representative memory pressure.
- `vm.swappiness=0` does not disable swap; it only avoids initiating swap until free plus file-backed pages fall below the zone high watermark.
- If the system mixes zram and disk-backed swap, one global swappiness cannot encode different costs per device; 133 assumes the swap IO actually used is the 2x-faster device.

question: X25
answer:
Default node-port range

The kube-apiserver flag --service-node-port-range has the upstream default value 30000-32767, inclusive at both ends. Therefore, when the API server is started without any port-range flag, the effective NodePort range is:

  30000-32767

For a Service of type NodePort with spec.ports[*].nodePort unset, the control plane dynamically allocates a free port from this configured range. Under the default range, dynamic allocation uses the upper band first, so the initially allocated port comes from 30086-32767; only after that band is exhausted does the allocator fall back to the lower band.

Static/dynamic split of the default range

Kubernetes computes the band offset as:

  bandOffset = min(max(16, floor(rangeSize / 32)), 128)

For the default range:

  rangeSize = 32767 - 30000 + 1 = 2768
  bandOffset = min(max(16, 2768 / 32), 128)
             = min(max(16, 86), 128)
             = 86

So the bands are:

  Static band:  30000-30085   (86 ports)
  Dynamic band: 30086-32767   (2682 ports)

Check: 86 + 2682 = 2768, which is exactly the inclusive size of 30000-32767.

Allocation semantics

- Static allocation: the user explicitly sets nodePort. The requested port must be within the full configured range 30000-32767 and must be unused cluster-wide; otherwise Service creation fails. The lower/static band 30000-30085 is intended and preferred for such explicit allocations because it has lower collision risk with auto-allocation.
- Dynamic allocation: nodePort is unset. The allocator draws from the upper/dynamic band 30086-32767 by default and falls back to the lower/static band 30000-30085 only after the upper band is exhausted.
- The request-analysis assumption that the static band is the highest-numbered portion and the dynamic band is the lowest is inverted relative to upstream Kubernetes documentation and KEP-3668. Upstream uses static = lower band, dynamic = upper band.
- One KEP ASCII line says 'Static band ends: 30086'; that is an off-by-one typo. The canonical documentation and the worked example table use static 30000-30085 and dynamic 30086-32767, consistent with bandOffset 86.

Direct answers

1. Default allocated range: 30000-32767.
2. Split under that default: static band 30000-30085 (86 ports), dynamic band 30086-32767 (2682 ports).

question: X28
answer:
## Answer

Per RFC 9293, Section 3.7.1 (Maximum Segment Size Option):

| Case | Default send MSS to assume when no MSS option is received | Derivation given by the RFC | Requirement level | RFC 9293 label |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| IPv4 | **536** | 576 - 40 | **MUST** | MUST-15 |
| IPv6 | **1220** | 1280 - 60 | **MUST** | MUST-15 |

**Ask 1 — IPv4 default send MSS: 536 octets.**
**Ask 2 — Requirement level: MUST** (normative label MUST-15; the same MUST applies to the IPv6 value 1220).

### Normative text (RFC 9293, §3.7.1)

> TCP endpoints MUST implement both sending and receiving the MSS Option (MUST-14).
>
> TCP implementations SHOULD send an MSS Option in every SYN segment when its receive MSS differs from the default 536 for IPv4 or 1220 for IPv6 (SHLD-5), and MAY send it always (MAY-3).
>
> If an MSS Option is not received at connection setup, TCP implementations MUST assume a default send MSS of 536 (576 - 40) for IPv4 or 1220 (1280 - 60) for IPv6 (MUST-15).
>
> The maximum size of a segment that a TCP endpoint really sends, the "effective send MSS", MUST be the smaller (MUST-16) of the send MSS (that reflects the available reassembly buffer size at the remote host, the EMTU_R [19]) and the largest transmission size permitted by the IP layer (EMTU_S [19]):
>
> Eff.snd.MSS = min(SendMSS+20, MMS_S) - TCPhdrsize - IPoptionsize
>
> where:
> * SendSMS is the MSS value received from the remote host, or the default 536 for IPv4 or 1220 for IPv6, if no MSS Option is received.
> * MMS_S is the maximum size for a transport-layer message that TCP may send.

(The checklist form of the same requirement reads: "IPv4 Send-MSS default is 536 — MUST-15" and "IPv6 Send-MSS default is 1220 — MUST-15".)

### Derivation of the two numbers

- **IPv4:** the IPv4 minimum datagram/reassembly size a host must support is 576 octets. Subtract the 20-octet IPv4 header and the 20-octet TCP header (40 total): 576 - 40 = **536**.
- **IPv6:** the IPv6 minimum MTU is 1280 octets. Subtract the 40-octet IPv6 header and the 20-octet TCP header (60 total): 1280 - 60 = **1220**. (IPv6 has no header checksum and no variable-length header at the base MTU, but RFC 9293 counts 60 octets of headers, not 40+20+extension headers.)

These are *segment data* sizes (MSS excludes the TCP header), which is why the header lengths are subtracted.

### Requirement-level precision (the part that is easy to get wrong)

Three distinct requirements sit next to each other in §3.7.1 and must not be conflated:

1. **MUST-14** — endpoints MUST implement sending *and* receiving the MSS option at all.
2. **SHLD-5** (SHOULD) — an implementation SHOULD *send* an MSS option in every SYN when its **receive** MSS differs from the default 536 (IPv4) / 1220 (IPv6); **MAY-3** allows sending it always. This is about emitting the option, not about the fallback value.
3. **MUST-15** (MUST) — if no MSS option is received at connection setup, the endpoint **MUST** assume the default **send** MSS of 536 (IPv4) / 1220 (IPv6). This is the ask, and it is unconditional MUST for both address families.

So: the *sending* of the option is SHOULD/MAY; the *fallback assumption* is MUST. The requirement level asked for is **MUST**.

### Implementation recipe (what a conforming stack must do)

```text
# At connection setup, per-connection state:
#   send_mss_default = 536  if address family == AF_INET
#                      1220 if address family == AF_INET6

on SYN_received_or_sent(tcb, seg, af):
    opt = parse_mss_option(seg.options)          # MUST-14: parse it
    if opt is present and valid (kind=2, len=4):
        tcb.SendMSS = opt.value                  # peer's advertised receive MSS
    else:
        tcb.SendMSS = (536 if af == AF_INET else 1220)   # MUST-15

    # MUST-16: clamp against the IP layer's send limit
    tcb.EffSndMSS = min(tcb.SendMSS + 20, tcb.MMS_S) - 20 - tcb.IPOptionsSize

# When emitting our own SYN:
    if our_receive_mss != (536 if af == AF_INET else 1220):
        emit MSS option = our_receive_mss          # SHLD-5
    # else: optional                                 # MAY-3
```

Notes for the implementer:
- `SendMSS` is the *peer's* advertised value (what we may send); the default applies only when the peer's SYN carried no MSS option. Do not use the local receive MSS as a substitute.
- `MUST-16` still applies on top of the default: the effective send MSS is `min(SendMSS+20, MMS_S) - TCPhdrsize - IPoptionsize`. With the IPv4 default and no IP options this evaluates to `min(556, MMS_S) - 20` = 536 whenever `MMS_S >= 556`; PMTUD/PLPMTUD may reduce it further for a specific path. The default is a *ceiling assumption about the peer's reassembly buffer*, not a promise to put 536 data octets on every path.
- The default is symmetric in intent (it protects the peer's receive buffer) but asymmetric in value by address family; a dual-stack listener must select 536 or 1220 per-connection based on the address family actually in use, not on a global configuration value.

### Conformance test vectors

| # | Scenario | Expected |
|---|---|---|
| T1 | IPv4 SYN received, no MSS option | SendMSS = 536 (MUST-15) |
| T2 | IPv6 SYN received, no MSS option | SendMSS = 1220 (MUST-15) |
| T3 | IPv4 SYN received, MSS option = 1460 | SendMSS = 1460 (option overrides default) |
| T4 | IPv6 SYN received, MSS option = 1440 | SendMSS = 1440 |
| T5 | IPv4, no MSS option, MMS_S = 1500, no IP options | Eff.snd.MSS = min(556, 1500) - 20 = 536 |
| T6 | IPv6, no MSS option, MMS_S = 1500, no IP options | Eff.snd.MSS = min(1240, 1500) - 20 = 1220 |
| T7 | IPv4, no MSS option, path MTU drops to 296 | Eff.snd.MSS reduced below 536 by the IP-layer clamp (MUST-16) |
| T8 | Local receive MSS = 536 on IPv4 | Sending the MSS option is optional (SHLD-5 not triggered; MAY-3 applies) |
| T9 | Local receive MSS = 1460 on IPv4 | SHOULD send MSS option = 1460 in SYN (SHLD-5) |

### Scope notes

- The authoritative source used is RFC 9293, which obsoletes RFC 793 and updates/absorbs the relevant RFC 1122 host requirements. The values 536 and 1220 and the MUST level are as stated in RFC 9293 §3.7.1; predecessor documents phrased the IPv4 default the same way but did not have the IPv6 default or the MUST-15 label.
- "Default send MSS" here means strictly the segment-size assumption used when the peer's SYN carried no MSS option. It is distinct from (a) the local *receive* MSS the endpoint advertises, and (b) the *effective* send MSS after the MUST-16 clamp against the IP layer.
