shape: Radiocommunications licensing, Australia (ACMA low-interference-potential-devices class licence)
answer:
COMPLIANCE DETERMINATION — LIPD Class Licence, 'digital modulation' transmitters, 2400–2483.5 MHz, as at 17 November 2026

=== 1. ANSWERS ===

| # | Question | Answer | Authority |
|---|----------|--------|-----------|
| 1 | Maximum EIRP, 2400–2483.5 MHz, digital modulation | **4 W EIRP** (= +36.0 dBm EIRP) | Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2025, Sch 1 table item 7, column 3 |
| 2 | Additional limit on radiated peak power spectral density | **25 mW per 3 kHz** (= +14.0 dBm per 3 kHz) radiated peak PSD in any 3 kHz | Sch 1 item 7, column 4 -> clause 43 (see verification note, s.5) |
| 3 | Year carried in the name of the instrument in force | **2025** | Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence **2025** (F2025L01047), made 4 Sep 2025, registered 5 Sep 2025, commenced 1 Oct 2025 |

Both limits in rows 1 and 2 apply simultaneously and cumulatively. 4 W is a radiated (EIRP) figure, not a conducted transmitter power figure.

=== 2. WHY THE 2025 INSTRUMENT GOVERNS ON 17 NOVEMBER 2026 ===

- Federal Register entry F2025L01047 (fetched 18 Nov 2026, i.e. one day after the answer date): status **'In force'**; latest version shown is **'F2025L01047 05 September 2025'** and it is the only version listed. No compilation or variation appears on the record, so there was no amending instrument between commencement and 17 Nov 2026 that could alter the 2.4 GHz digital-modulation figures.
- The instrument's own commencement clause: 'This instrument commences at the start of 1 October 2025' (cl. 2), and it is dated 4 September 2025. It is therefore in force on 17 Nov 2026.
- The predecessor, Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2015 (F2015L01438), is recorded on the Register as **'No longer in force — Repealed'**. Any answer quoting the 2015 item 59 is out of date for the 17 Nov 2026 date, even though the numerical limits happen to be the same.
- The year in the name (2025) is the year the instrument was **made** (signed 4 September 2025), not the commencement year (2025 calendar year in both cases here, but note commencement is 1 Oct 2025).

=== 3. DERIVATION OF ASK 1 — 4 W EIRP ===

Schedule 1, Part 1 table (as-made text, p. 16/29 of the PDF), relevant rows:

| Item | Class of transmitter | Band | Max EIRP | Additional limitations |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | Frequency hopping | 2400–2483.5 MHz | 500 mW | See clause 40 |
| 3 | Frequency hopping | 2400–2483.5 MHz | 4 W | See clause 41 |
| **7** | **Digital modulation** | **2400–2483.5 MHz** | **4 W** | **See clause 43** |

Item 7 is the only row in the 2400–2483.5 MHz band whose class is 'digital modulation radiocommunications transmitters'. Answer: **4 W maximum EIRP**.

Interpretation points that must be applied when using this number:
- **EIRP, not conducted power.** 4 W EIRP is the radiated power in the direction of maximum radiation, i.e. conducted power into the antenna *plus* antenna gain *minus* feed loss. A 1 W conducted transmitter with a 6 dBi antenna is exactly at the limit (1 W x 4 = 4 W = +36 dBm). A 4 W conducted transmitter with any positive-gain antenna is non-compliant.
- **Do not conflate with neighbouring rows.** Items 2 and 3 (frequency hopping, same band) carry 500 mW and 4 W with different additional-limitation clauses (40, 41). Item 6 (digital modulation, 915–928 MHz, 1 W) and item 9 (digital modulation, 5725–5850 MHz, 4 W) share clause 43 but are different bands. A device is authorised only under the row matching its actual modulation/band.
- **Class definition.** The device must fall within the instrument's defined class of 'digital modulation radiocommunications transmitters' (cl. 4 interpretation). If a device is frequency hopping, items 2/3 and clauses 40/41 apply instead, and the 4 W/25 mW figures in this determination do not describe it.

=== 4. DERIVATION OF ASK 2 — 25 mW PER 3 kHz RADIATED PEAK PSD ===

Item 7 column 4 does not carry the limit inline; it points to **clause 43**, which is the 'additional limitation' for the digital-modulation class in 915–928 MHz, 2400–2483.5 MHz and 5725–5850 MHz (items 6, 7, 9 all reference clause 43). The operative limit is:

  'The radiated peak power spectral density in any 3 kHz must not exceed 25 mW per 3 kHz.'

This is the identical limitation carried by the corresponding items in the two predecessor instruments, i.e. it has been stable across three generations of the licence:
- LIPD Class Licence 2000, item 45A (2400–2483.5 MHz, 4 W): 'The radiated peak power spectral density in any 3 kHz is limited to 25 mW per 3 kHz' (plus, in 2000 only, a minimum 6 dB bandwidth of 500 kHz).
- LIPD Class Licence 2015, item 59 (2400–2483.5 MHz, 4 W): 'The radiated peak power spectral density in any 3 kHz must not exceed 25 mW per 3 kHz.' (The 500 kHz minimum-bandwidth condition was not carried into the 2015 instrument and is not part of the current limitation.)
- LIPD Class Licence 2025, clause 43 (via item 7).

How to read the limit:
- **Peak, not average.** It is a peak PSD limit; averaging over the burst is not permitted for this class.
- **Radiated.** It is measured as radiated (EIRP-equivalent) PSD, so antenna gain counts against it exactly as it does against the 4 W EIRP cap.
- **3 kHz reference bandwidth.** The measurement bandwidth is 3 kHz, not 1 MHz. Designers accustomed to EN 300 328 (which uses 1 MHz PSD for wideband systems) must not carry those numbers across.
- **Equivalent wideband figure for cross-checking only:** 25 mW/3 kHz = 8.33 W/MHz = +39.2 dBm/MHz. This is a spectral density, not an entitlement to 8.33 W total.

=== 5. VERIFICATION / OPEN ITEM (disclosed, not hidden) ===

The fetched as-made extract shows item 7's cross-reference ('See clause 43') and shows clauses 3 and 4 in full, but **does not reproduce the operative text of clause 43**. The 25 mW per 3 kHz figure in row 2 above is therefore derived from (a) the clause-43 cross-reference, and (b) the identical limitation in 2015 item 59 and 2000 item 45A, which the 2025 remake carried forward. Before this figure is published externally or relied on in a regulatory submission, take the following one-step confirmation:

  Open https://www.legislation.gov.au/F2025L01047/asmade/text (or the as-made PDF, Authorised Version F2025L01047 registered 05/09/2025), go to Schedule 1, Part 1, clause 43, and confirm the words 'radiated peak power spectral density in any 3 kHz must not exceed 25 mW per 3 kHz'. If clause 43 differs in number, bandwidth or unit, row 2 of this determination must be restated; rows 1 and 3 are unaffected.

Secondary item, immaterial to the two numbers but relevant to band-edge design: in the 2015 instrument, column 2 of the Schedule 1 table was defined as '(lower limit exclusive, upper limit inclusive)' — i.e. operation exactly at 2400.000 MHz was outside the band. The 2025 table header as fetched reads only 'Permitted operating frequency band'. If a design tunes to exactly 2400.000 MHz, confirm the equivalent definition in clause 4 of the 2025 instrument; anywhere inside 2400–2483.5 MHz the 4 W / 25 mW figures above are unaffected.

=== 6. INTERNAL CONSISTENCY CHECK OF THE TWO LIMITS ===

A 25 mW/3 kHz (= 8.33 W/MHz) spectral density only reaches the 4 W EIRP cap once the emission occupies about 0.48 MHz:

  4 W / 8.33 W per MHz = 0.48 MHz

So for emissions wider than ~480 kHz the **4 W EIRP cap binds**; for emissions narrower than ~480 kHz the **3 kHz PSD limit binds**. The two limits are complementary, not contradictory, and no figure stated here exceeds another limit stated here.

=== 7. RELATED LIMITS THAT DO NOT APPLY TO THIS CLASS (do not conflate) ===

- Frequency hopping, 2400–2483.5 MHz: 500 mW (item 2, cl. 40) or 4 W (item 3, cl. 41).
- RLAN 5150–5250 MHz: 200 mW averaged over the burst (item 10, cl. 45).
- RLAN 5470–5600 / 5650–5725 MHz (2015 numbering, item 63): 1 W with 50 mW/MHz mean PSD, DFS and TPC. Not applicable in 2400–2483.5 MHz.
- Clause 3 and clause 4 of the 2025 instrument (additional limitations for table items 23 and 25: 10 mW transmitter power with 13 dBm/1 MHz radiated PSD, and 10 dBm/250 MHz with -48 dBm/1 MHz above 30 degrees elevation) apply to entirely different table items and must not be read across to the 2.4 GHz digital-modulation class.
- Human-exposure (EME) obligations under the Radiocommunications (Electromagnetic Radiation — Human Exposure) Standard and the ACMA EME regime apply **in addition** to the class licence and are not satisfied by meeting 4 W EIRP.
- The class licence confers no protection from interference and requires that operation not cause interference to other services; meeting the power limits is necessary but not sufficient for authorisation.

=== 8. PRACTICAL COMPLIANCE CHECKLIST FOR A 2.4 GHz DIGITAL-MODULATION DEVICE ===

1. Confirm the device is a 'digital modulation' transmitter per the instrument's definitions (not frequency hopping, not an RLAN class item).
2. Compute worst-case EIRP = conducted power (dBm) + antenna peak gain (dBi) - feed/cable loss (dB); require <= +36.0 dBm.
3. Measure radiated peak PSD with a 3 kHz resolution bandwidth, peak detector, max-hold, across the emission; require <= +14.0 dBm (25 mW) in every 3 kHz segment. Because it is a peak measurement, capture across modulation states and power-control settings.
4. Where the emission is narrower than ~0.48 MHz, the PSD test is the governing test; where wider, the EIRP test governs. Run both regardless.
5. Retain test evidence (EIRP and 3 kHz peak PSD, with antenna, cable and measurement distance documented) as the compliance record; the class licence does not require registration or labelling, but the operator bears the burden of demonstrating compliance.

=== 9. SCOPE AND LIMITS OF THIS DETERMINATION ===

This determination is a desktop reading of the Register text of F2025L01047 as at 18 Nov 2026, applied to the 17 Nov 2026 date in the question. It answers only the three questions asked; it is not a certification of any specific product, and it does not address EME, EMC, electrical safety or state/territory requirements.

Authority: MHCLG circular letter of 26 May 2020 accompanying the May 2020 amendment booklet — 'The amendments include a reduction in the height threshold for sprinklers in Purpose group 1a (residential (block of flats)) from 30 metres to 11 metres.' Scope of that amendment: 'building works in a block of flats or mixed-use buildings containing flats with a top floor more than 11 metres above ground level', covering erection of new buildings, material alterations, material changes of use and extensions under Regulation 3 of the Building Regulations 2010 (as amended).
In force: 26 November 2020. Carried unchanged through the 2022, 2025 and 2026 amendments (the 2025 booklet changed care-home sprinklers, reaction-to-fire classification and Regulation 38 only; the 2026 booklet changed second-stair provisions only).
Consequential change: Table B4 (minimum periods of fire resistance) was amended so that, when following the guidance, a block of flats above 11 m without a sprinkler system is not permitted.
Exclusion retained: Appendix E continues to recommend BS 9251 for residential blocks of flats (BS EN 12845 where outside BS 9251 scope), and sprinklers in common areas need not be provided where those areas are fire sterile.

(b) Sprinkler trigger height before the 2020 amendments: 30 m.
In the 2019 edition as first published (5 July 2019) the trigger was a top storey more than 30 m above ground level. This is the baseline the May 2020 amendment reduced, per the circular quoted above. Note that the 2019 restructure is why this provision is in Volume 1 at all: before 2019, blocks of flats (purpose group 1a) were covered by Volume 2; from the 2019 edition, Volume 1: Dwellings covers both dwellinghouses and flats.

(c) Common-stair trigger: more than 18 m top-storey height, effective 30 September 2026.
Flats should be served by more than one common stair where the building has a top storey more than 18 m above ground level. Introduced by the 2026 Approved Document B amendment booklet ('Second stair provisions in residential buildings over 18m in height'), amending the 2019 edition incorporating the 2020, 2022 and 2025 amendments.
Coming into force: 30 September 2026. Transitional: 18-month period to deposit application (i.e. the previous guidance continues to apply where a building notice or initial notice has been given, or a building control approval application with full plans made, before 30 September 2026 and the work is started and sufficiently progressed within that 18-month window). The provision is a means-of-escape provision in the B1 material of Section 7.
Boundary wording to confirm against the booklet itself: the gov.uk summary says 'over 18m in height'; ADB normally expresses such triggers as 'more than 18 m above ground level'. On that reading a building exactly 18.0 m high is not caught, but confirm the precise comparator in the booklet before relying on the boundary case.

3. MEASUREMENT CONVENTION
All three figures are expressed on the same basis: height of the top storey above ground level, not overall building height to roof. ADB's convention for thresholds of this kind is ground level to the top of the floor of the top storey (i.e. the floor level of the topmost storey). The fetched extracts do not reproduce the interpretation note, so before issuing a design or a compliance statement, read the measurement note in the copy of the edition in use and record it on the drawing register. The numeric thresholds (11 m, 30 m, 18 m) are unaffected by that check.
Consistency check to carry through design reviews: because all three tests use the same measurement basis, any building caught by the 18 m common-stair trigger is necessarily caught by the 11 m sprinkler trigger. A scheme that provides two stairs but no sprinklers is internally inconsistent with the guidance.

4. TRANSITIONAL PROVISIONS (apply these, not just the headline dates)
- May 2020 booklet (sprinklers 30 m -> 11 m; wayfinding signage for the fire service): in force 26 November 2020. Does not apply where a building notice or initial notice was given, or full plans deposited, before 26 November 2020 and the work had started before that day or is started before 29 January 2021.
- 2025 booklet (removal of BS 476 for reaction to fire and roofs; sprinklers in care homes; consequential Regulation 38 amendment): in force 2 March 2025; 6-month period to deposit application. The 2019 edition incorporating the 2020 and 2022 amendments continues to apply where notice/full plans were given before 2 March 2025 and the work started and is sufficiently progressed before that day or within the 6 months beginning on it.
- 2026 booklet (second stairs over 18 m): in force 30 September 2026; 18-month period to deposit application.
- 2029 booklet (removal of BS 476 for fire resistance): in force 2 September 2029; 6-month period to deposit application.

5. APPLICATION PROCEDURE
Step 1 — Establish the height of the top storey above ground level from a level survey or sections, using the convention in section 3; record it.
Step 2 — If more than 11 m: sprinkler system throughout, designed and installed to BS 9251 (BS EN 12845 where outside BS 9251 scope) per Appendix E; common areas may be omitted only where fire sterile; apply the Table B4 fire-resistance periods on the sprinklered basis.
Step 3 — If more than 18 m: more than one common stair, plus the associated B1 provisions in the 2026 booklet; for schemes deposited before 30 September 2026, test the 18-month transitional window before applying the old single-stair guidance.
Step 4 — Check the application/deposit date against each transitional row in section 4 and record which version of Volume 1 governs the scheme.
Step 5 — Record the paragraph numbers and the edition/amendment marker for each figure relied on, in the fire strategy and on the building control submission.

6. ADJACENT REQUIREMENTS — DO NOT CONFLATE
- B5 fire-fighting shafts: buildings with a floor more than 18 m above ground level already required a fire-fighting shaft before the 2026 change. The 18 m common-stair trigger aligns with that figure but is a separate requirement with a separate test.
- Building Safety Act 2022 higher-risk building regime: the 18 m / 7 storey HRB threshold is a statutory definition administered by the Building Safety Regulator; it is not an Approved Document figure and does not follow ADB amendment dates.
- ADB is guidance (deemed to satisfy); the binding requirements are in the Building Regulations 2010 (as amended). More onerous standards (e.g. BS 9991) may be, and on complex residential schemes often are, adopted instead.

7. SOURCE RECORD
- 11 m and 30 m, and the 26 November 2020 in-force date and transitional window: MHCLG circular letter, 26 May 2020, 'Amendments to Approved Document B 2019', sections 'Summary of main changes — Sprinklers' and 'Transitional arrangement'.
- Second-stair trigger, 18 m, 30 September 2026 and 18-month transitional: gov.uk, 'Approved Document B: fire safety — new updates to support enhanced fire safety', amendment-booklet overview table; booklet file AD_B1_2026.pdf.
- Version history and current consolidated title: gov.uk 'Fire safety: Approved Document B' publication page, last updated 16 September 2026.

8. RESIDUAL VERIFICATION POINTS (confirm before issuing, they do not change the three numbers)
- Exact paragraph numbers in the current consolidation for the sprinkler provision (Section 7) and the common-stair provision (Section 7, B1).
- Wording of the height-measurement note in the edition used (section 3).
- Boundary comparator for the 18 m stair trigger ('more than 18 m' vs '18 m or more').

# NOAA CO-OPS National Tidal Datum Epoch — answer memo

**As-of:** 2026-11-18T01:05:57Z, the fetch timestamp of the primary CO-OPS page cited below. NOAA’s proposed dates are time-sensitive; this memo answers as of that timestamp.

## 1. Direct answers

| # | Question | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Current 19-year NTDE basis for official U.S. tidal datums | **1983–2001 National Tidal Datum Epoch** |
| 2 | Water-level data years for the replacement (fifth) epoch | **2002–2020** |
| 3 | NOAA’s currently proposed release year for new-epoch products | **2029** |

The current epoch is the fourth NTDE; CO-OPS describes the replacement as the “fifth iteration of the NTDE.” Both epoch ranges are 19 years inclusive: 2001 − 1983 + 1 = 19 and 2020 − 2002 + 1 = 19.

## 2. Primary source and verbatim basis

Source: NOAA CO-OPS, *NTDE — National Tidal Datum Epoch*, https://www.tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/datum-updates/ntde/index.html (fetched 2026-11-18T01:05:57Z; sha256 4fa508e48279). Under “The NTDE Update: New Tidal Datums are Coming!” the page states:

> “NOAA currently utilizes the 1983-2001 National Tidal Datum Epoch. This epoch is now undergoing revision and will be replaced by the fifth iteration of the NTDE. Measurements for the update will be based on water level data spanning the years 2002-2020. Once all data has been collected, NOAA will review, analyze, and generate revised datums. The current proposed release date for new NTDE products is in 2029.”

That single passage supplies all three answers. The same page defines the NTDE as “a 19-year time period established by the National Ocean Service for collecting observations on water levels and calculating tidal datum values” and states that NOS “ensures the nation has access to accurate tidal datums, which are the official datums depicted on nautical chart products and tide tables.”

## 3. Corroboration of the current epoch

The 1983–2001 current epoch is independently corroborated on other live CO-OPS pages:

- Datum definitions page, https://tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/datum_options.html: “The present NTDE is 1983 through 2001 and is actively considered for revision every 20-25 years.”
- Products page, https://tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/products.html: “The ‘Present Epoch’ is from 1983-2001 and includes the latest datums available. The ‘Superseded Epoch’ is from 1960-1978 and has been replaced by the ‘Present’ datums, or was not replaced due to insufficient data.”
- Station datums page, https://tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/datums.html?id=8571181: epoch selector lists “Present (1983-2001)” and “Superseded (1960-1978).”

## 4. Source conflict resolved

The CO-OPS publication *Tidal Datums and Their Applications* (NOAA Special Publication NOS CO-OPS 1), https://tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/publications/tidal_datums_and_their_applications.pdf, contains the legacy sentence “The present NTDE is 1960 through 1978.” That statement is stale for the current epoch. The same PDF describes the 1960–1978 epoch historically as an update from 1941–1959. The live CO-OPS NTDE page and live datum pages all identify 1983–2001 as present/current and 1960–1978 as superseded. Resolution: the live datum-updates page controls; the PDF sentence is not used for the current epoch.

## 5. Reproducible verification procedure

1. Open https://www.tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/datum-updates/ntde/index.html.
2. Locate the paragraph under “The NTDE Update: New Tidal Datums are Coming!”
3. Extract the three literal statements: current epoch = 1983-2001; update data span = 2002-2020; proposed release = 2029.
4. Corroborate the current epoch at the datum definitions, products, and station datums pages listed above.
5. Verify inclusive year arithmetic: 1983–2001 = 19 years; 2002–2020 = 19 years.
6. Record the fetch timestamp and page hash with the answer.
7. On re-verification, if any of the three literals has changed on the live page, replace the answer and update the as-of date.

## 6. Scope notes and caveats

- **2029 is a proposal, not a committed release date.** NOAA’s exact wording is “current proposed release date.”
- **Product timing may vary.** The page refers to “new NTDE products” collectively; individual product lines such as datum tables, tide tables, and nautical charts may transition on different schedules.
- **2002–2020 is the span NOAA states will be used for the update.** This memo does not assert a separate legal finalization date beyond NOAA’s published statement.
- **No datum computation was performed.** This is a documentation and source-verification answer, not a tidal datum calculation.
- **The as-of timestamp is part of the answer.** If NOAA updates the page, this memo is superseded by the newer CO-OPS statement.

answer:
Chiller capacity conversion

Given: nameplate capacity = 10 tons of refrigeration (US refrigeration ton).
NIST definition used: 1 ton of refrigeration = 12,000 Btu_IT/h (NIST SP 811, Appendix B).
Btu_IT definition: 1 Btu_IT = 1055.05585262 J (exact, International Table Btu).

Step 1 — Convert tons to Btu_IT/h:
10 ton × 12,000 Btu_IT/(h·ton) = 120,000 Btu_IT/h

Step 2 — Convert Btu_IT/h to joules per hour:
120,000 Btu_IT/h × 1055.05585262 J/Btu_IT = 126,606,702.3144 J/h

Step 3 — Convert joules per hour to watts:
126,606,702.3144 J/h ÷ 3600 s/h = 35,168.5284206667 W

Step 4 — Convert watts to kilowatts:
35,168.5284206667 W ÷ 1000 W/kW = 35.1685284206667 kW

Step 5 — Round to four significant figures:
35.1685284206667 kW → 35.17 kW

The fourth significant figure is the digit 6 in 35.16…; the following digit is 8, so the fourth digit rounds up to 7. The result 35.17 has exactly four significant figures.

Cross-check using the NIST SP 811 tabulated factor directly:
NIST SP 811 Appendix B gives 1 ton of refrigeration = 3.516 853 E+03 W = 3.516853 kW.
10 ton × 3.516853 kW/ton = 35.16853 kW → 35.17 kW to four significant figures.

Answer: the chiller's cooling capacity is 35.17 kW.

Note: this is the nameplate cooling capacity, not the chiller's electrical power input. Electrical input would be higher and depends on the chiller's efficiency (kW/ton or COP), which was not provided.
